title: Round Trips & the arcsin(sin x) Trap

steps.body: One composition direction is always safe: **sin(arcsin v) = v** for every v in [−1, 1] — arcsin outputs a branch angle, and sine happily eats it. The reverse, **arcsin(sin x)**, equals x ONLY when x already lies in the branch [−π/2, π/2]. Outside it, the round trip returns a different angle (recall the same one-way trap from verifying inverses).

predict.prompt: arcsin(sin 150°): sine of 150° is 1/2. Does the round trip return 150°?

options.label: No — arcsin can only answer from inside its branch: you get 30° back
Yes — inverse means you always get your angle back

predict.reveal: You get 30°. sin(arcsin x) is the SAFE direction — 0.3 in, 0.3 out, as above — but arcsin(sin θ) must answer from inside [−90°, 90°], and 150° lives outside. Try to drag to 150°: the wall you hit is the fold happening under your hand.

widget.prompt: Try to reach 150° — then settle for what arcsin actually returns: the angle INSIDE the branch that shares 150°'s sine.
widget.successFeedback: 30° — the branch's representative for sine 1/2. The wall at 90° is why arcsin(sin 150°) = 30°, not 150°: the round trip folds everything back into the arc where the inverse is allowed to live. sin(arcsin 0.3) = 0.3 has no such fold — that direction never leaves home.
widget.lowFeedback: Sine is below 1/2 here — climb. (150° stays unreachable however hard you push the wall; that push IS the lesson.)
widget.highFeedback: Sine is above 1/2 — ease back to 30°, the one angle this branch offers for that sine.

explanationVariants: sin(5π/6) = 1/2, then arcsin(1/2) = π/6 — the branch angle with the SAME sine, not the angle you started with.
5π/6 is outside [−π/2, π/2]; arcsin can only answer with in-branch angles, so it returns π/6.

options.label: π/6
options.feedback: Right — the sine collapses to 1/2 and arcsin returns the BRANCH angle for 1/2: π/6, not 5π/6.

options.label: 5π/6
options.feedback: arcsin's outputs live in [−π/2, π/2]; 5π/6 ≈ 2.62 can never come out. The trip lands on π/6.
1/2 is the intermediate SINE value. arcsin turns it back into an angle: π/6.

steps.body: When the round trip IS safe.
explanationVariants: 0.4 rad already lies inside [−π/2, π/2], so arcsin(sin(0.4)) = 0.4 exactly.
In-branch angles survive the trip unchanged — that's what inverse-on-its-branch means.

commonErrors.feedback: You may be rounding the intermediate sin(0.4) ≈ 0.389 — but no rounding survives an exact inverse: 0.4 lies inside the branch, so the round trip returns 0.4 itself.
Nothing flips: sin(0.4) ≈ 0.389 is positive, and its branch angle is +0.4 itself.

steps.body: The general rule: **arcsin(sin x)** answers *"which BRANCH angle has the same sine as x?"* For second-quadrant x, that's the mirror **π − x**; the same logic gives arccos(cos x) = the [0, π] angle sharing x's cosine. Compositions of DIFFERENT functions, like cos(arcsin v), come next.

explanationVariants: x = 5π/3 is in Quadrant IV; sin(5π/3) = −√3/2, and subtracting a full turn gives the branch angle 5π/3 − 2π = −π/3.
sin(5π/3) = −√3/2, so arcsin(−√3/2) = −π/3 — the branch angle sharing that sine.

options.label: −π/3
options.feedback: Right — sin(5π/3) = −√3/2, and the branch angle sharing that sine is −π/3 (subtract a full turn to land inside the branch).

options.label: 5π/3
options.feedback: 5π/3 ≈ 5.24 is far outside the branch [−π/2, π/2]. Subtracting 2π gives the branch angle: −π/3.

options.label: −2π/3
options.feedback: That uses the π − x mirror, which only works when x is between π/2 and 3π/2. Here subtract 2π instead: 5π/3 − 2π = −π/3.

explanationVariants: sin(7π/6) = −1/2 (Quadrant III), and arcsin(−1/2) = −π/6 — the branch handles negative sines with negative angles.
The branch angle sharing sine −1/2 is −π/6; 7π/6 itself is far outside [−π/2, π/2].
hints: First: what is sin(7π/6)? (Quadrant III — sign matters.)
Recall arcsin(−1/2) from the arcsine lesson.

options.label: −π/6
options.feedback: Right — the sine is −1/2, and the branch's angle for −1/2 is −π/6.

options.label: 7π/6
options.feedback: 7π/6 ≈ 3.67 is way outside the output fence [−π/2, π/2]. The trip lands at −π/6.

options.label: π/6
options.feedback: Sign check: sin(7π/6) = −1/2, NEGATIVE — so the branch angle is −π/6.

steps.body: One direction is a promise; the other, a question.
takeaways: arcsin(sin x) = x only for x in [−π/2, π/2]; otherwise it returns the branch angle with x's sine.
Quadrant II inputs map to π − x; negative sines map to negative branch angles.
steps.teaser: Next: mixed compositions — cos(arcsin v) and the triangle that solves them.

concept.body: To evaluate arcsin(sin x): compute the sine, then ask which angle IN [−π/2, π/2] has that sine. The answer is x itself only when x is already in the branch.

explanationVariants: sin π = 0 and arcsin(0) = 0 — not π, which is outside the branch.
The branch angle with sine 0 is 0.

commonErrors.feedback: π is outside [−π/2, π/2]: arcsin can't return it. sin π = 0, and arcsin(0) = 0.
sin π = 0 (not 1): the trip gives arcsin(0) = 0.
